source_refs.note: Chapter 11 exercise (PDF 269-272) solved: 13 MCQs keyed from the chapter (no key printed), 12 short questions (b in three parts; k and l with structures written as condensed formulas) and 4 descriptive questions. Book corrections: Q.2(k)(x), Q.2(l) labels.

blocks.prompt: I. An alkene undergoes ozonolysis followed by reduction with zinc dust and water to yield propanone and methanal. The alkene is:
blocks.explanation:
Ozonolysis cuts the C=C and puts C=O on each carbon (11.8.1). Joining the two carbonyl carbons back: (CH₃)₂C=O + O=CH₂ come from (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, 2-methylpropene.
(CH₃)₂C=CH₂ + O₃ → ozonide → (Zn/H₂O) (CH₃)₂C=O + HCHO

blocks.prompt: II. Which of the following reagents is typically used for the acid-catalyzed hydration of alkenes to form alcohols?
blocks.explanation: Hydration adds H₂O across C=C with an acid (H₂SO₄) catalyst: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O → (H₂SO₄) C₂H₅OH (11.8.1). H₂/Ni hydrogenates, O₃ cleaves, Br₂ brominates.

blocks.prompt: III. Halogenation of alkanes is an example of:
blocks.explanation: Alkanes react with Cl₂ or Br₂ in UV light through free radicals (initiation, propagation, termination), replacing H by halogen (11.5.1).

blocks.prompt: IV. Which of the following reactions can an alkane undergo?
blocks.explanation: Alkanes are saturated (no π bond), so they cannot add or polymerize; they undergo free radical substitution (and combustion, cracking) (11.5).

blocks.prompt: V. What is the first step in the electrophilic addition reaction of alkenes?

options.text: Attack by an electrophile on the double bond

blocks.explanation: The π electrons of C=C attack the electrophile first; this gives the carbocation, which is then attacked by the nucleophile (11.8.1).

blocks.prompt: VI. The addition of unsymmetrical reagent to an unsymmetrical alkene is in accordance with the rule/principle?
blocks.explanation: Markovnikov's rule: the negative part of the reagent attaches to the double-bonded carbon that bears fewer hydrogens (11.8.1).

blocks.prompt: VII. The most stable carbonium ion among the following is:
blocks.explanation: Carbonium ion is the older name of a carbocation. (CH₃)₃C⁺ is tertiary: three alkyl groups push electrons (+I effect) towards C⁺, so stability is 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl (11.7.2).

blocks.prompt: VIII. Markownikov’s rule is applicable to :
blocks.explanation: The rule applies only to an unsymmetrical alkene. (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ is unsymmetrical; ethene and 2-butene are symmetrical, and propane (b) has no double bond (11.8.1).

blocks.prompt: IX. What intermediate is formed during the electrophilic addition of HBr to an alkene?
blocks.explanation: H⁺ from HBr adds to one carbon of C=C, leaving a carbocation that Br⁻ then attacks (11.8.1).

blocks.prompt: X. The enhanced stability of conjugated dienes compared to isolated dienes is primarily attributed to:

options.text: Inductive effects of the double bonds.
Increased s-character of the hybridised orbitals.
Delocalisation of π electrons across the conjugated system.
Steric hindrance between the double bonds.

blocks.explanation: In a conjugated diene the p orbitals of adjacent carbons overlap, so the π electrons are delocalised over the whole system, which stabilises the molecule (11.9).

blocks.prompt: XI. Which of the following carbocations would be the least stable?
blocks.explanation: The methyl carbocation CH₃⁺ has no alkyl group to donate electrons (+I) to the positive carbon, so it is the least stable (11.7.2).

blocks.prompt: XII. Which of the following is the repeating unit in the polymer poly(ethene) (polyethylene)?
blocks.explanation: The repeating unit is the monomer CH₂=CH₂ with the C=C changed to a C−C single bond: −CH₂−CH₂− (11.8.1). (d) is the unit of poly(propene).

blocks.prompt: XIII. Which type of structural isomerism involves differences in the arrangement of the carbon skeleton?
blocks.explanation: Chain isomerism arises from a difference in the carbon chain, e.g. butane and 2-methylpropane (C₄H₁₀) (11.10.1).

blocks.prompt:
a. Define the following:
i) Cycloalkanes ii) Isomerism iii) Conjugated dienes iv) Inductive effect
blocks.explanation:
i) Cycloalkanes: saturated cyclic aliphatic hydrocarbons (CₙH₂ₙ) whose carbon atoms form a ring of single bonds, e.g. cyclopropane C₃H₆.
ii) Isomerism: two or more compounds having the same molecular formula but different structural formulas and properties, e.g. butane and 2-methylpropane.
iii) Conjugated dienes: dienes in which the two C=C double bonds are separated by one single bond, e.g. CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂.
iv) Inductive effect: the polarization of a σ bond due to the electron-withdrawing (−I, e.g. halogen) or electron-donating (+I, e.g. alkyl) effect of adjacent atoms or groups.

blocks.prompt:
b. Differentiate between:
i) Aliphatic and Aromatic hydrocarbons
blocks.explanation: Aromatic hydrocarbons are based on the benzene ring; all others are aliphatic.

rows: Not based on benzene; open chain or cyclic
Based on benzene (C₆H₆) or similar rings

blocks.prompt: b. ii) Homolytic and Heterolytic Fission
blocks.explanation: Both break a covalent bond; they differ in how the shared electron pair is divided.

rows: Bond breaks evenly: each atom takes one electron
One atom takes both shared electrons

blocks.prompt: b. iii) Electrophile and Nucleophile
blocks.explanation: An electrophile seeks electrons; a nucleophile supplies them.

rows: Negative or has a lone pair or π electrons, written Nu:⁻
Attacks electron-rich sites such as C=C
Attacks electron-poor sites such as a carbocation
e.g. H⁺, Br⁺ (δ⁺ Br of Br₂)
e.g. OH⁻, Br⁻, an alkene's π bond

blocks.prompt: c. Explain why alkanes do not undergo addition reactions.
blocks.explanation: Alkanes are saturated: each carbon already has four single σ bonds and there is no π bond to break, so no atom can be added. They can only react by replacing an H atom (substitution).

blocks.prompt: d. How elimination reaction is considered the opposite of an addition reaction.
blocks.explanation: In addition, atoms add across C=C and the alkene becomes saturated; in elimination, a small molecule is removed from adjacent carbons and a C=C is formed. One reverses the other.

rows: Atoms or groups are added across C=C
A small molecule (H₂O, HX) is removed from adjacent carbons
π bond is broken; unsaturated → saturated
π bond is formed; saturated → unsaturated
e.g. CH₃CH₂Br + KOH(alc) → CH₂=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O

blocks.prompt: e. Compare the carbocation stability in propene and 2-butene.
blocks.explanation:
Propene (unsymmetrical) can give a 2° carbocation, CH₃CH⁺CH₃ (more stable, two +I methyl groups), or a 1° carbocation, CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺ (less stable); so it gives a major and a minor product.
2-Butene (symmetrical) gives the same 2° carbocation, CH₃CH⁺CH₂CH₃, whichever carbon is attacked, so only one product forms. Both main carbocations are secondary and of similar stability.

blocks.prompt: f. Given the molecular formula C₅H₁₀, list all possible structural isomers that are alkenes.
blocks.explanation:
Five alkene structural isomers:
1. CH₂=CH–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃, pent-1-ene
2. CH₃–CH=CH–CH₂–CH₃, pent-2-ene
3. CH₂=C(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₃, 2-methylbut-1-ene
4. CH₂=CH–CH(CH₃)–CH₃, 3-methylbut-1-ene
5. (CH₃)₂C=CH–CH₃, 2-methylbut-2-ene
(Pent-2-ene also has cis and trans forms; that stereoisomerism is in the Class 12 syllabus.)

blocks.prompt: g. When propene (C₃H₆) undergoes electrophilic addition with HBr, it forms 2-bromopropane as the major product. Explain why 2-bromopropane is favored over 1-bromopropane, using the concept of carbocation stability.
blocks.explanation: H⁺ can add to either carbon of C=C. Adding to the CH₂ end gives the 2° carbocation CH₃CH⁺CH₃, stabilized by the +I effect of two methyl groups; adding to the middle carbon gives the less stable 1° carbocation CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺. The more stable 2° ion forms faster and Br⁻ attacks it, giving 2-bromopropane (Markovnikov's rule).

blocks.prompt: h. Explain why conjugated alkenes may show different reactivity compared to isolated alkenes.
blocks.explanation: In conjugated alkenes the p orbitals on adjacent carbons overlap and the π electrons are delocalised over the whole system. This makes them more stable and changes how they react, e.g. buta-1,3-diene polymerizes to give rubber-like polymers. In isolated alkenes each C=C reacts on its own, like a simple alkene.

blocks.prompt: i. Explain how inductive effects from alkyl groups stabilize carbocations in alkenes.
blocks.explanation: Alkyl groups are electron donating (+I). They push σ-bond electrons towards the positive carbon, which spreads (reduces) its positive charge and makes the ion more stable. More alkyl groups mean more stability: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl carbocation.

blocks.prompt: Q.3 Describe the free radical halogenation of methane using Cl₂ as an example.
blocks.explanation:
Methane reacts with chlorine in sunlight or UV light; H atoms are replaced by Cl atoms through free radicals: CH₄ + Cl₂ → (UV) CH₃Cl + HCl.
Mechanism:
1. Initiation: UV light breaks the Cl–Cl bond homolytically: Cl₂ → (hν) Cl• + Cl•
2. Propagation: CH₄ + Cl• → •CH₃ + HCl; then •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•. The new Cl• repeats the cycle (chain reaction).
3. Termination: two radicals combine: •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl; •CH₃ + •CH₃ → CH₃–CH₃ (traces of ethane, evidence of free radicals); Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂.
Further substitution: with more chlorine, propagation repeats: CH₃Cl → CH₂Cl₂ (dichloromethane) → CHCl₃ (trichloromethane, chloroform) → CCl₄ (tetrachloromethane). The more Cl₂ at the start, the more highly chlorinated the products.

blocks.prompt:
Q.4 Describe the following methods for the preparation of alkenes:
i) Dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides
ii) Dehydration of alcohols
blocks.explanation:
Both are elimination reactions: a small molecule is removed from adjacent carbon atoms, creating a C=C double bond.
i) Dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides: an alkyl halide is heated with alcoholic KOH; H and the halogen are removed from adjacent carbons as HX.
H₃C–CH₂–Br + KOH(alcoholic) → (heat) H₂C=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O
ii) Dehydration of alcohols: ethanol heated with excess concentrated H₂SO₄ at 180 °C loses a water molecule.
CH₃CH₂OH → (conc. H₂SO₄, 180 °C) CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O
It takes place in two steps through ethyl hydrogen sulphate:
CH₃CH₂OH + H₂SO₄ → CH₃CH₂OSO₃H + H₂O
CH₃CH₂OSO₃H → (heat) H₂C=CH₂ + H₂SO₄ (the acid is regenerated).

blocks.prompt: Q.5 Describe the mechanism of electrophilic addition of hydrogen halides to alkenes. Discuss Markovnikov’s Rule in the context of hydrogen halide addition.
blocks.explanation:
Alkenes react with dry gaseous hydrogen halides at room temperature to give haloalkanes; the rate increases HF < HCl < HBr < HI. H–X is polar (Hδ⁺–Xδ⁻), so H is the electrophile.
Mechanism (ethene + HBr):
Step 1: the π electrons of C=C attack the δ⁺ H of HBr; H–Br breaks heterolytically giving Br⁻, and a carbocation forms: CH₂=CH₂ + H–Br → CH₃–CH₂⁺ + Br⁻
Step 2: the nucleophile Br⁻ attacks the carbocation: CH₃–CH₂⁺ + Br⁻ → CH₃–CH₂–Br (bromoethane)
A symmetrical alkene gives only one product.
Markovnikov's rule: when a polar reagent adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the negative part of the reagent attaches to the double-bonded carbon that bears fewer hydrogens.
Propene + HBr: H⁺ adds to the CH₂ end, giving the more stable 2° carbocation CH₃–CH⁺–CH₃ (two +I methyl groups); Br⁻ attacks it to give 2-bromopropane (major). Addition through the less stable 1° carbocation CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺ gives 1-bromopropane (minor).
CH₃–CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃–CHBr–CH₃ (major) + CH₃–CH₂–CH₂Br (minor)

blocks.prompt:
Q.6 Explain the following reactions of alkenes with examples:
a) Halogenation b) Ozonolysis
c) Epoxidation d) Polymerization
blocks.explanation:
a) Halogenation: addition of Cl₂ or Br₂ across C=C. Bromine in CCl₄ (red-brown) is decolourised at once by ethene, a test for unsaturation.
CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → Br–CH₂–CH₂–Br (1,2-dibromoethane)
Mechanism: the C=C repels the Br–Br electrons, so the near Br becomes δ⁺ (electrophile); the π electrons attack it, forming a carbocation and Br⁻; Br⁻ then attacks the carbocation.
b) Ozonolysis: ozone cleaves the C=C to form an ozonide, which Zn/H₂O reduces to carbonyl compounds (aldehydes or ketones).
C₂H₄ + O₃ → C₂H₄O₃ (ozonide) → (Zn/H₂O) 2HCHO
CH₃CH=CH₂ + O₃ → ozonide → (Zn/H₂O) CH₃CHO + HCHO
The carbonyl products show where the double bond was, so it is used to find the structure of an unknown alkene.
c) Epoxidation: an oxidizing agent adds one O atom across C=C, giving an epoxide (a three-membered cyclic ether). Ethene with O₂ over a silver catalyst gives ethylene oxide; acid hydrolysis converts it to ethane-1,2-diol.
CH₂=CH₂ + ½O₂ → (Ag) ethylene oxide (CH₂–CH₂ ring with O) → (H⁺/H₂O) HOCH₂–CH₂OH
d) Polymerization (addition): many monomers with a C=C join into a long chain as the only product; each π bond breaks and new C–C single bonds form.
n CH₂=CH₂ → –[CH₂–CH₂]ₙ– (poly(ethene))
n CH₂=CHCl → –[CH₂–CHCl]ₙ– (PVC)
Used for bags, bottles, packaging and pipes.
